tagline: A state capital that just proved urban water transit works: the relaunched Baía de Vitória ferry carried over 1.2 million riders in under three years, the government is building three more stations — and the signature run glides straight under the Terceira Ponte.
summary: Greater Vitória wraps around the Baía de Vitória — the capital sits on an island, Vila Velha faces it across the bay mouth, and Cariacica sits up the northwest channel, so nearly every daily trip funnels over a handful of bridges (the Terceira Ponte alone carries roughly 90,000 vehicles a day). In August 2023 the Espírito Santo state government relaunched passenger boats on the bay after two decades dormant: 500,000 riders in year one, more than 1.2 million by December 2025, four stations, six catamarans, and R$61.8 million committed to three more stations. This is a government actively scaling water transit on sheltered urban water — exactly the setting where electric foiling adds speed, silence and zero emissions over a bay ringed by port cranes, colonial landmarks and Brazil's most celebrated urban mangrove.

use_cases.title: Foiling layer on a proven transit bay
use_cases.body: Fast, silent 12–15-seat shuttles woven into the existing 401/402/403 station pattern — Prainha, Praça do Papa, Rodoviária, Porto de Santana — adding frequency between the big catamarans' sailings and extending service hours, inside the same Cartão GV fare system.

use_cases.title: Bay, landmarks and mangrove
use_cases.body: Foiling circuits past the Convento da Penha, Morro do Moreno, the port cranes, Palácio Anchieta and the Cinco Pontes, ending at Ilha das Caieiras' waterfront moqueca restaurants on the edge of the urban mangrove — silent and zero-wake where diesel tour boats churn today.

use_cases.title: Business-district water shuttle
use_cases.body: Enseada do Suá and Praia do Canto hold the state's corporate towers, the Iate Clube do Espírito Santo and the marina scene — a premium point-to-point layer linking them to Vila Velha and the airport side of the island without touching the bridge queue.

use_cases.title: Beach-island spider
use_cases.body: Short premium hops to Curva da Jurema, Ilha do Boi and Ilha do Frade — the capital's most exclusive waterfronts, minutes from the stations but a world away by road at rush hour.

journeys.from: Prainha (Vila Velha, Estação Governador Albuíno Azeredo)
journeys.to: Praça do Papa (Vitória, Estação Prefeito Setembrino Pelissari)
journeys.today: A diesel catamaran roughly every 24 minutes, or a car crawl over the Terceira Ponte with 90,000 other vehicles a day.
journeys.with_navier: A silent electric foiling glide under the Terceira Ponte — the bay's signature crossing, minutes dock to dock, with the Convento da Penha above the stern.

journeys.today: Line 401's catamaran down the winding bay channel, or a long congested drive around the bay through city streets.
journeys.with_navier: A fast, smooth foiling run the full length of the Baía de Vitória — past the Cinco Pontes, the port cranes and the old town waterfront — in a fraction of the road time.

journeys.today: The newest station (May 2026) links the intercity bus terminal to the bay — but on the same diesel catamarans and headways.
journeys.with_navier: Arrive by intercity bus, board a foiling shuttle, and be at the Praça do Papa waterfront in minutes — a genuinely multimodal arrival into the capital.

journeys.today: A drive across town to the northwest shore, or a slow tour-boat leg — the famous moqueca restaurant row is a destination without a fast water link.
journeys.with_navier: A foiling hop up the bay and into the Santa Maria river mouth, arriving silent and zero-wake at the mangrove's edge for lunch — the gastronomy run every visitor will want.

journeys.from: Iate Clube do Espírito Santo (Praia do Canto)
journeys.today: A drive over the bridge at rush hour, though the two waterfronts stare at each other across the bay mouth.
journeys.with_navier: A short foiling hop around Ilha do Boi and across the bay mouth — club pontoon to the historic Vila Velha waterfront below the Convento da Penha.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire metro mesh is ultra-short — 0.6 to ~5 nm legs between Prainha, Praça do Papa, Rodoviária, Porto de Santana, Ilha das Caieiras and the Praia do Canto marina cluster — trivially inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope, with shore charging at the state's own stations. Pioneer II serves the premium spurs (Curva da Jurema, Ilha do Boi, Ilha do Frade, Iate Clube) while the N35 Shuttle's 12–15 seats, shallow 1.5 ft draft and enclosed cabin slot naturally into the scheduled 401/402/403 pattern as a frequency and off-peak layer alongside the catamarans.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR's 700 nm hybrid range opens the Espírito Santo coast beyond the bay with no charging dependency — south to Guarapari's beaches (~30 nm) and Anchieta, north toward the Doce river coast — turning the capital's proven bay network into the hub of a state coastal corridor.

competitive_landscape: The water is run today by the state's own relaunched aquaviário — six diesel catamarans managed under CETURB-ES across four stations, integrated with the Transcol bus network — plus a lively leisure fleet: shared lancha operators like Capitão Grilo (R$139–169 a seat), schooner tours (R$30–60) and private charters from the Iate Clube and Marina Bay Vix. That is demand evidence, not saturation: 1.2 million transit riders and a paying tour market on the same sheltered water, currently served at ~24-minute headways by conventional diesel hulls. A foiling layer upgrades speed, quietness and emissions on routes the public already votes for daily.
seasonality: Year-round operation on sheltered water. Austral summer (Dec–Mar) is hot and wet with afternoon thunderstorms and peak beach demand; winter (Jun–Sep) is dry, mild and calm. The Baía de Vitória is protected in nearly all conditions; southeasterly cold fronts can put wind chop on the bay mouth and the ocean-side beaches — exactly the sea state foiling flies over. No cyclone exposure.
regulatory_note: A single motivated state government owns the whole stack: SEMOBI (state mobility and infrastructure secretariat) sets policy and builds the stations, CETURB-ES manages operations and the Cartão GV fare integration, and vessel certification sits with the Brazilian Navy's Capitania dos Portos do Espírito Santo. The state is mid-expansion (R$61.8M, three new stations, 'soon seven stations'), and the bay's northwest arm holds one of Brazil's largest urban mangrove systems — a concrete case for silent, zero-emission, low-wake vessels as the fleet grows.
signature_routes: Prainha ↔ Praça do Papa — the bay-mouth crossing under the Terceira Ponte (the signature visual)
Porto de Santana ↔ Praça do Papa — the full-bay run past the Cinco Pontes, the port and the old town
Praça do Papa ↔ Ilha das Caieiras — the mangrove gastronomy run to the moqueca waterfront

precedents.why_it_matters: Proof that electric foiling can be the backbone of a scheduled water-transport network at national scale — the playbook a state already investing in water transit can replicate.
